1.why: The reset token is verified only against the recovery record stored in the current session and tied to an existing account.

2.why: A reset token is accepted only when the current session has a matching live recovery record, so it is not valid for any other user.

3.why: Password reset changes the account hash but does not revoke or delete other existing sessions, so prior authenticated sessions can remain valid.

4.why: HTTPS/TLS is configured and enforced, but the code does not specify or prove the latest TLS protocol version.

5.why: TLS protects data in transit and passwords/token hashes use strong algorithms, but reset codes and in-memory user data are not explicitly encrypted at rest.

6.why: No real email is sent; the simulated delivery does not include private user data, but it does expose the recovery code and email behavior is not implemented.

7.why: User inputs are constrained by validation patterns and rendered via textContent, although there is no general-purpose sanitization library.

8.why: The application only uses same-origin API calls and hash-based navigation, with no external redirect targets.

9.why: No email templates are present, so unsafe user-controlled email HTML or scripts cannot be observed.

10.why: The client-side logs and console output display mock recovery tokens and MFA codes.

11.why: Passwords are bcrypt-hashed, but the MFA code is a hardcoded plaintext value used as a secret.

12.why: The startup password is random, but the fixed MFA code functions as a default second-factor secret.

13.why: Login, recovery-code verification, and MFA verification all lock or throttle after repeated failed attempts.

14.why: The recovery page embeds the mock account/reference identifier in the form, revealing that identifier to any visitor.

15.why: The reset token is generated with randomBytes, has a long base64url format, and is bound to the session/account recovery record.
